column2: There too there is no contentment on seeing a still more radiant fortune. So all these destinations have been told distinctly.
Now I shall tell the origin of the embryo; hear it attentively as I tell it truly, brahmin.
As a fruit tree when it bears gives much fruit, so merit done with a pure mind becomes vast.
Sin likewise comes from sin done with an evil mind; for the self acts in action with the mind placed first.
Hear further how a man, covered by desire and anger, as directed by his deed, enters the womb.
Semen mixed with blood, having gone into a woman's womb, gains a field born of deeds, good or bad.
Because of subtlety and unmanifest nature it clings nowhere; having attained the body of Brahman, that Brahman is eternal, the seed of all beings, by which creatures live.
That soul, entering all the limbs of the embryo in parts, and abiding in the seats of life, at once supports them with consciousness; then the embryo, endowed with consciousness, moves its limbs.
As molten iron poured in takes the shape of the mould, know that to be the entry of the soul into the embryo.
As fire enters a lump of iron, heating it all, know likewise the soul's coming into the embryo.
Service to mother and father, honouring gods and guests, worship of teachers, compassion, purity, constant restraint of the senses,
and doing what is good: this is called the conduct of the good. From it dharma arises, which protects creatures forever.
Thus one should always look to the good, for there is the fixed standing; conduct shows dharma, in which the good are established.
That which is set down as dharma in them is eternal dharma; one who attains it does not meet a bad end.
Therefore the bewildered world is held to the paths of dharma; but the yogi and the liberated are distinguished from these.
For a man living in dharma, in due course after a great time his crossing of rebirth comes.
Thus every creature enjoys its earlier deed; that is the cause by which this one has come here, cut out.
By whom was the taking of a body planned before? So is the doubt in the world, and I shall tell that next.
Having made the body for the self, Brahma, grandsire of all beings, created the whole three worlds, moving and unmoving.
Then he created Pradhana, the consciousness of embodied beings, by which all this is pervaded, which the world knows as supreme.
Here it is called perishable; the supreme is the imperishable immortal; the pair of the three is all, each one separate.
The first-created Prajapati created all beings and the immovable beings; so says the ancient tradition.
The Grandsire fixed the measure of time for it, the turning among beings and their return.
As a wise one here, who has seen the self in a past birth, what I shall tell is all rightly fitting.
One who always sees pleasure and pain as impermanent, and the body as a mass of filth, subject to destruction and tied to action,
and remembers that whatever pleasure there is is all sorrow, will cross the terrible ocean of rebirth, so hard to cross.
Entered by birth, death and disease, knowing Pradhana, he sees consciousness as the same in conscious beings and in all.
Then, tired of all, seeking the supreme state, I shall tell you the teaching on it truly, best of men.
Hear, brahmin, entire, the supreme knowledge of the eternal, imperishable state as I declare it.
A friend to all, enduring all, equal in attachment, master of his senses, free of fear and anger, slayer of desire, a man is freed.
One who lives among all beings as with himself, restrained, pure, without conceit and pride, is freed everywhere.
Life and death, pleasure and pain, gain and loss, the dear and disliked: he who is equal in these is freed.
He who longs for nothing, despises nothing, free of dualities, his self free of passion, is freed everywhere.
One who somewhere has no enemy, no kin, no offspring, who has given up dharma, wealth and desire, and is free of expectation, is freed.
Neither righteous nor unrighteous, shedding what was earlier accumulated, his self calmed by the wasting of the elements, free of dualities, he is liberated.
Without action, without wishes, seeing the world as impermanent, unhealthy, helpless, ever deluded by birth and rebirth,
his mind turned to dispassion, ever looking at the faults of torment, he soon accomplishes release from the bonds of the self.
An ascetic who has given up resolves, free of hypocrisy and ego, a wise brahmin sees the Self in the Self by the mind.
If this good man can yoke the Self in the Self, then, devoted to solitude, he sees the Self in the Self.
Restrained, ever disciplined, self-possessed, master of his senses, he thus rightly sees the Self by the self.
As a man who, in a dream, sees and then sees "that is he," so, well joined, he sees the Self as of that form.
As one might draw out a reed from a clump of munja grass and show it, so the yogi sees the Self drawn out within the body.
They say the munja is the body and the reed rests in the Self; this is the highest example given by knowers of yoga.
When the embodied one rightly sees the Self yoked, then no one rules him, even he who is lord of the three worlds.
He takes other bodies as he wishes; turning away from old age and death, he neither rejoices nor grieves.
The joined one, self-mastered, makes even the gods' godhood happen; leaving the impermanent body, he attains imperishable Brahman.
Even when the worlds perish, fear does not arise in him; when beings are suffering, he is not made to suffer by any.
The joined self, free of longing, calm of mind, would not be shaken by terrible things made of sorrow and grief born of attachment and affection.
Weapons do not pierce him, and he has no death; there is nothing happier than this anywhere in the world.
When he has rightly yoked the Self and sees the Self in the Self, then he does not long for the position even of Shatakratu himself.
One who is practising yoga should never give way to disgust; hear how one devoted to solitude should practise yoga.
Thinking of the direction seen before, the city he lives in, his mind should be inside the city, not outside.
Staying inside the city, in whatever dwelling he lives, he should hold his mind in that dwelling, within and without.
Having thought of the whole dwelling, in the body where he abides, his mind should be in that body and in no way outside.
Restraining the host of senses, in a silent, lonely forest, he should contemplate the whole body within, one-pointed.
He should think of teeth, palate, tongue, throat, neck, and heart, and the binding of the heart.
[Brahmin] Thus told by me, Madhusudana, that wise pupil asked again about this hard-to-explain dharma of liberation:

How is the food eaten, again and again, digested in the stomach? How does it become juice, how is blood born, and how does it nourish flesh, fat, sinews and bones?
mahabharata:14:19.38	How do all these bodies of embodied beings grow, and how does strength grow in one who grows? How do the waste products, devoid of essence, depart, each separately?
mahabharata:14:19.39	Whence does this breath go out, and breathe in again? And in what place does this Self abide in the self?
mahabharata:14:19.40	How does the soul carry the body, moving the corpse-like frame? What colour, of what kind, does the mind establish? Tell me truly, blessed one, blameless.
Thus asked by that brahmin, Madhava, I answered, mighty-armed scourge of foes, as I had heard.
As one who has put goods into his storeroom thinks of the vessels, so, having placed the mind in his body through steady doors, he should seek the Self there and avoid carelessness.
Thus, ever diligent, glad of soul, he soon reaches that Brahman, seeing which one would know Pradhana.
It is not grasped by the eye or by all the senses; by the mind alone, as a lamp, the great Self is seen in the self.
With hands and feet everywhere, eyes, heads and mouths everywhere, the soul sees the Self departed from the body.
Giving up his body, holding only Brahman, he beholds the Self with the mind, as if smiling.
This whole secret I have told you, best of brahmins; I take leave and shall accomplish; go, pupil, as you please.
Thus told by me then, Krishna, that pupil of great austerity, the brahmin with doubts cut, went as he wished.
[Vasudeva] Having said these words to me then, Partha, that chief of brahmins, standing rightly in the dharma of liberation, vanished right there.
Partha, have you heard this with a one-pointed mind? For then too, seated in the chariot, you heard just this.
This, Partha, is not easily understood by one with a mixed mind, I think, nor by a man of unformed notions, clever or of unformed self.
This great secret of the gods has been told, best of the Bharatas; I hope it has not been heard by any other mortal, Partha.
No other man is fit to hear this, blameless one, but you; it is not easily understood today with a mixed inner mind.
The world of the gods is full of the active, son of Kunti; and the gods do not like mortals turning back from forms.
That is the highest goal, Partha, which is eternal Brahman, where one attains immortality, giving up sorrow, ever happy.
Resting thus in dharma, even those who are of sinful birth, women, vaishyas and shudras, go to the highest goal.
How much more brahmins and kshatriyas, Partha, learned, ever delighting in their own dharma, devoted to Brahma's world?

This has been set forth with reasons: the means for accomplishing it, the fruit of perfection, liberation, and the decision about sorrow. What happiness would there be other than this, best of the Bharatas?
A mortal, learned, faithful and valiant, who gives up the worldly business as worthless, by these means quickly reaches the highest goal.
This much is to be said; there is nothing more. For one constantly disciplined, yoga, Partha, goes forward in six months.
A brahmin woman, seeing a brahmin versed in knowledge and wisdom seated in solitude, said to her husband:

To what world shall I go, having taken refuge in you as husband, you who sit with actions laid aside, a peasant, unskilled?
mahabharata:14:20.4	We have heard that wives gain worlds made by their husbands; having reached you as husband, to what goal shall I go?
So addressed, the calm-souled one said to her, as if smiling: "Fortunate one, I do not find fault with this word, blameless one.
What is graspable, seen and heard, this action that there is: doers of action determine this alone as action.
Those without knowledge restrain only delusion by action; actionlessness is not found in this world, even for a moment.
By deed, mind and word, good or bad, action goes on among beings, in the distinction of forms from birth onward.
While actions with visible objects are being killed by demons, I saw the abode resting in the self, by that self."
Among all of them, eating one another and moving among the gods, the Vaishvanara fire is set in seven ways in the middle.
Nose, tongue, eye, skin, ear as fifth, mind and intellect: these seven are the tongues of Vaishvanara's flames.
What is smelled, drunk, seen, touched and heard, what is to be thought, what is to be known: those seven are my kindling sticks.
The smeller, the eater, the seer, the toucher, the hearer as fifth, the thinker and the knower: these seven are the chief priests.
In the smellable, drinkable, visible, touchable and audible, the offerers, sevenfold, wisely putting oblations in the seven fires, produce in their own wombs.
Earth, wind, space, water, fire as fifth, mind and intellect: these seven are spoken of as wombs.
All the qualities, being oblations, enter the fire-born mouth; having dwelt within, they are born in their own wombs, and there are stopped at dissolution, the source of beings.
From that smell is born, from that taste is born, from that form is born, from that touch is born.
From that sound is born, doubt arises there, from that determination is born; they know this birth as sevenfold.
In this very way, taken up by the ancients, those filled with full oblations are filled with radiance.
Everything here is to be known; the mind looks to knowledge. Semen is the body-bearer in the body, while the knower is the body-bearer.
The body-bearer is the Garhapatya; another is led forth from it, then the Ahavaniya, and into it the oblation is thrown.
From that arose the lord of speech; Samana looks on; form becomes manifest, and the mind runs after it.
[Brahmin woman] "Which came first, speech or mind? When a thought of the mind comes to be spoken,
by what union of knowledge is the understanding established in thought? Raised up, it did not get through; who obstructs it?"
[Brahmin] "Apana, becoming its lord, directs it from there to the state of Apana; they call it the understanding of the mind, and from that the mind looks.
Since you ask me about the question of speech and mind, therefore I shall tell you the dialogue between those two.
Both speech and mind went and asked the Self of beings, 'Tell us which of us is better, lord, and cut our doubt.'"
Between prana and apana, the goddess Speech always stood; urged on, fair one, unable to move without prana, she ran to Prajapati: "Be gracious, blessed one."
Then prana appeared, refreshing speech again; therefore, having reached the exhaling breath, speech never speaks.
The sounding one, having produced sound, goes on forever; and of those two sounding ones, the soundless is greater.
She flows like a cow, the best yielder of essence, ever streaming, this eternal speaker of Brahman.
By divine and undivine power, pure-smiling one, Bharati is the cow; see the difference between these two subtle streaming ones.
When no sentences had arisen yet, urged by desire to create, which then did the goddess Sarasvati utter first?
She who arises in the body with prana, from prana reaches apana, and, as udana, leaving the body, with vyana covers all of heaven,
then stands established in samana here; so she first said. Therefore the mind is superior for being immovable, and the goddess is superior for being moving.
Nose, eye and tongue, skin, ear as fifth, mind and intellect: these seven offerers are each separately settled.
Being in subtle space, they do not see one another; know these seven offerers, fair one, by their nature.
[Brahmin woman] "How, being in subtle space, do they not see one another? How are they of their own nature? Tell me this, blessed lord."
[Brahmin] "Ignorance of qualities, lack of knowledge, knowing the possessor of the quality, awareness: these never know one another's qualities.
Tongue, eye, ear, skin, mind and intellect do not reach smells; the nose reaches them.
Nose, eye, ear, skin, mind and intellect do not reach tastes; the tongue reaches them.
Nose, tongue, ear, skin, mind and intellect do not reach forms; the eye reaches them.
Nose, tongue, eye, ear, intellect and mind do not reach touches; the skin reaches them.
Nose, tongue, eye, skin, ear and mind do not reach the settled conclusion; the intellect reaches it.
On this too they cite an ancient tale, fair one: the dialogue between the senses and the mind.
[Mind] 'Without me the nose does not smell, the tongue does not know taste, the eye does not grasp form, the skin does not know touch.
The ear does not know sound without me in any way; I am the eternal best of all beings.
Without me the senses do not shine, like empty houses or fires with their flames calmed.
Like wet and dry wood, though the senses strive, all creatures do not reach the objects of the qualities without me.'
[The senses] 'This would be true as you think, if without us you enjoyed the pleasures that are our objects.
If, when we are dissolved, you enjoy pleasures and tastes, nourishing and sustaining life, then it is as you think.
Or, when we are dissolved and objects remain, if by mere resolve you enjoy pleasures as they are.
If you think you succeed in our objects always, take form by the nose, take taste by the eye,
take smell by the ear, take certainty by the tongue, take sound by the skin, and touch by the intellect.
The strong are without rules and the rules are for the weak; take pleasures never before taken; you should not eat what is left over.
As a pupil runs to his teacher for the meaning of the scripture, and then takes what is heard and attends to its meaning,
so you think of objects shown by us, future and past, in dream and waking.
In creatures of little mind who have fallen into dejection, life is seen sustained when the work is done for our sake.
Though you think of many resolves and enjoy dreams, pressed by hunger you run only to objects.
Entering a house as if without a door, enjoying by resolve, finding no objects, at the failing of life you always find peace, like a fire lit when the wood is spent.
True, we are attached to our own qualities, and our qualities are not mutually perceived; without us there is no perception of you, and without you, joy would not serve us.'"
Prana, apana, udana, samana and vyana: these five offerers the wise know as the supreme state.
[Brahmin woman] "That the offerers are seven by nature was your earlier view. As the offerers are five, say what the supreme state is."
[Brahmin] "The wind gathered by prana becomes apana; the wind gathered in apana goes on as vyana.
The wind gathered by vyana then goes on as udana; the wind gathered in udana goes on as samana.
They once went and asked Prajapati, born first: 'Tell us which of us is eldest; he will be best for us.'
[Brahma] 'He in whose dissolution all the vital breaths in the bodies of embodied beings go to dissolution, and by whose going about they move again, he is the best; go where you wish.'
[Prana] 'When I am dissolved, all the vital breaths in the bodies of embodied beings go to dissolution, and when I move they move again. I am the best; see me dissolved.'
[Brahmin] Prana was dissolved, and then moved again; samana and udana then spoke, fair one.
'When I am dissolved, all the vital breaths in the bodies of embodied beings go to dissolution, and when I move they move again. I am the best; see me dissolved.'
Vyana and udana spoke to him as he spoke: 'Apana, you are not the best, for prana is in your control.'
Apana then moved, and vyana again said to him: 'I am the best of all; hear the reason.
When I am dissolved, all the vital breaths in the bodies of embodied beings go to dissolution, and when I move they move again. I am the best; see me dissolved.'
Then vyana was dissolved and moved again; prana, apana, udana and samana said to him: 'You are not the best, vyana, for samana is in your control.'
Vyana moved again, and samana spoke again: 'I am the best of all; hear the reason.
When I am dissolved, all the vital breaths in the bodies of embodied beings go to dissolution, and when I move they move again. I am the best; see me dissolved.'
Then samana was dissolved and moved again; prana, apana, udana and vyana said to him: 'Samana, you are not the best, for vyana is in your control.'
Samana moved, and udana said to him: 'I am the best of all; hear the reason.
When I am dissolved, all the vital breaths in the bodies of embodied beings go to dissolution, and when I move they move again. I am the best; see me dissolved.'
Then udana was dissolved and moved again; prana, apana, samana and vyana said to him: 'Udana, you are not the best, for vyana is in your control.'
Then Brahma, Prajapati, said to them as they stood together: 'All are best and none is best; all are mutually dependent. All are best in their own domain, and all protect one another.
One is steady and one unsteady; the five winds are distinguished by difference. My Self is one alone, though it is built up in many ways.
Friends of one another, bring each other into being; go in well-being; may it be well with you; uphold one another.'"
[The brahmin woman] "When a creature is being born, which goes first: prana, apana, samana, vyana or udana?"
[Brahmin] "That by which this creature is created, another goes before it. The pair of breaths should be known as the transverse and the upward.
[Woman] By what is this creature created, and which other goes before it? Tell me the pair of breaths, the transverse and upward, with certainty."
[Brahmin] "Joy is born from resolve, and from sound, from taste, from form,
from touch, and from smell. This is the form of udana; joy is born of the couple's union.
From desire semen is born, from desire the essence is born; in the common semen and blood produced by samana and vyana,
from semen mixed with blood, prana goes first; when the semen is changed by prana, apana then goes.
This pair, prana and apana, goes downward and upward; vyana and samana, both, are called the transverse pair.
His smoke is darkness, passion is ash, and goodness arises in the one of good seed, where the oblation is thrown.
The knowers of sacrifice know samana and vyana as the two pourings; prana and apana as the two portions of ghee, and between them the fire. Brahmins know this as the highest form of udana.
That which is free of dualities, hear it as I tell it.
Day and night are the pair, and between them the fire; brahmins know this as the highest form of udana.
The two courses are a pair, and between them the fire; brahmins know this as the highest form of udana.
Truth and falsehood are a pair, and between them the fire; brahmins know this as the highest form of udana.
Good and bad are a pair, and between them the fire; brahmins know this as the highest form of udana.
Being and non-being are a pair, and between them the fire; brahmins know this as the highest form of udana.
First samana and vyana are fixed, and by them the act is fixed; the third is again determined by samana.
For peace, the Vamadeva chant; peace is eternal Brahman. Brahmins know this as the highest form of udana."
The rule of all this will be taught by rule; hear it from me, fair one, as I tell this supreme secret.
Instrument, action, doer and liberation: these four, fair one, are the offerers by whom this world is covered.
Hear in full the means of the offerers: nose, tongue, eye, skin, ear as fifth, mind and intellect: these seven are to be known as causes of qualities.
Smell, taste, form, sound, touch as fifth, what is to be thought, what is to be known: these seven are causes of action.
The smeller, eater, seer, toucher, hearer as fifth, thinker and knower: these seven are to be known as causes of the doer.
These, possessing qualities, consume their own quality, good or bad; and "I am without qualities here": these seven are causes of liberation.
For the learned who are awake, each in its own place by rule, the qualities, becoming deities, constantly enjoy the oblation.
The unlearned who eats food comes to it with a sense of 'mine'; cooking always for himself, he is destroyed by 'mine'.
Eating what is not to be eaten and drinking liquor destroy him; he destroys the food and the food destroys him, and the wise man, having destroyed it, is destroyed.
The learned eater of this food produces again the lord; he is born from the food, and in that there is a subtle transgression.
What is reached by the mind and what is restrained by speech, what is heard by the ear and what is seen by the eye,
what is touched by touch and smelled by the nose: restraining all these oblations with the mind as sixth,

for me the fire, the oblation-carrier, burns with qualities. My yoga sacrifice is in progress, the knowledge of Brahman born of the mind; prana is the hymn, apana the recitation, with complete renunciation as the fee.
Brahma consents to my action, I am the doer and the Adhvaryu, the hymn is made, the instruction is made, that scripture, and liberation is its fee.
People who know Narayana also recite here the Rik verses about the animals bound to the god Narayana long ago.
There they sing Samans, and they call them proof. Know, timid one, the god Narayana as the Self of all."
[Brahmin] "There is one teacher and no second beyond him, who dwells in the heart; I speak of him. Instructed by that teacher always, all the danavas were defeated.
There is one kinsman and no second beyond him, who dwells in the heart; I speak of him. Instructed by him, kinsmen having a kinsman, the seven sages shine in heaven.
There is one hearer and no second beyond him, who dwells in the heart; I speak of him. Having lived as pupil with that teacher, Shakra went to the immortality of all worlds.

Pandava Bibhatsu will attend to the women and the children in time, and to your funeral rites.
